common_name: Orange Dream Japanese Maple (Bright Orange-Yellow Spring Foliage Maple)

planting.note: Plant container trees in early spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Orange Dream tolerates more direct sun than most yellow-leaved Japanese maple cultivars without scorching, though afternoon shade is still recommended in zone 8-9 gardens.

directions: Orange Dream is grown chiefly for its spring foliage display: the five-lobed leaves emerge a bright orange-yellow to golden orange, a color it tends to hold better in sun than most similarly bright cultivars, before mellowing to a soft yellow-green through summer and finishing with orange-red highlights in fall. The habit is a compact, upright-rounded small tree or large shrub, slower and denser than the species, making it well suited to smaller landscapes, mixed borders, and large containers. Unlike deep red-leaf cultivars such as Bloodgood, Orange Dream is prized specifically for extending the palette of Japanese maple color into warm gold and orange tones during the spring flush. In zone 9, give it moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil and afternoon shade to keep leaf edges from scorching during peak summer heat; consistent moisture during dry spells helps maintain foliage quality through the season.

common_name: Katsura Japanese Maple (Orange-Salmon Spring Foliage Maple)

planting.note: Plant container trees in early spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Katsura is a distinct, long-cultivated Japanese maple cultivar and is unrelated botanically to Cercidiphyllum japonicum, the tree commonly called 'katsura tree'.

directions: Katsura is one of the older, longer-established Japanese maple cultivars grown for its striking spring color: new leaves emerge in shades of orange, salmon, and soft yellow with fine reddish veining, a display that is most intense in cooler spring weather, before the leaves mature to light green through summer and finish in gold and orange tones in fall. Its upright, moderately vigorous habit forms a small tree or large multi-stemmed shrub with a graceful, slightly open branching structure. Because the spring color is more pronounced with some direct morning light, siting Katsura where it gets gentle morning sun and afternoon shade brings out the best color while still protecting foliage from summer scorch in hot climates. In zone 8, deep watering during establishment and mulching to keep roots cool are important, since Katsura's color intensity and leaf quality both suffer under prolonged heat stress.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)

common_name: Shishigashira Japanese Maple (Lion's Head Maple, Crinkled Dark Green Foliage)

planting.note: Plant container trees in early spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Shishigashira is exceptionally slow-growing, so choose the largest available container stock if a landscape-scale specimen is wanted within a reasonable timeframe.

directions: Shishigashira, the 'Lion's Head' maple, is one of the oldest recorded Japanese maple cultivars and is instantly recognizable by its small, densely congested, tightly curled and crinkled dark green leaves packed closely along stiff, upright branches, an effect that resembles a lion's ruffled mane and gives the tree unusual year-round textural interest even before fall color develops. Growth is very slow and dense, forming a compact, broadly columnar to oval small tree that rewards patience with an architecturally distinctive specimen well suited to formal gardens, entry plantings, and large containers. Fall color arrives later than most Japanese maples, often into November, in brilliant blends of gold, orange, and red that persist on the tree longer than the species type because the crinkled leaves resist wind loss. In zone 8, afternoon shade and consistent soil moisture help the dense canopy avoid leaf scorch during peak summer heat.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)

common_name: Shindeshojo Japanese Maple (Brilliant Fluorescent Pink-Red Spring Foliage Maple)

planting.note: Plant container trees in early spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Shindeshojo's fluorescent spring color is most vivid with some direct morning sun and is best protected from harsh afternoon sun in hot climates.

directions: Shindeshojo (sometimes sold as Shin Deshojo) produces some of the most vivid spring foliage of any Japanese maple cultivar: new leaves emerge in an almost fluorescent crimson-pink, brightest for the first several weeks of the growing season, before gradually settling to green with pink-tinged margins through summer and finishing in shades of red and orange in fall. The habit is a compact, upright-rounded small tree or large shrub, easily kept smaller with light pruning, which combined with its intense color has made it a favorite for container culture, bonsai, and small-space gardens. Because the brightest color depends partly on cool spring temperatures and morning sun exposure, siting Shindeshojo where it gets gentle early light and afternoon shade produces the best display while protecting the thin new leaves from scorch. In zone 8, watch for a secondary flush of red new growth in late summer, which is normal for this cultivar and adds a second color event to the season.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)

common_name: Sharp's Pygmy Japanese Maple (True Dwarf Mounding Maple)

planting.note: Plant container plants in early spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; as a true dwarf, Sharp's Pygmy is well suited to raised beds, rock gardens, troughs, and containers where its compact scale can be appreciated up close.

directions: Sharp's Pygmy is one of the true dwarf Japanese maple cultivars, growing extremely slowly into a dense, rounded, mounding cushion that rarely exceeds a few feet in height and width even after many years, in contrast to the tree-scale habit of most palmatum cultivars. The small, finely proportioned leaves emerge green in spring and turn orange-red in fall, held on a tight framework of fine branching that gives the mound a neat, tailored appearance year-round. Its scale makes it a popular choice for rock gardens, trough and container plantings, bonsai training, and the front of small ornamental beds where a full-size maple would overwhelm the space. Because dwarf cultivars have a smaller root mass relative to their dense canopy, keep the soil consistently moist and mulched, and give afternoon shade in zone 8 to prevent leaf scorch on the compact foliage.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)

common_name: Trompenburg Japanese Maple (Large Upright Maple with Cupped Reddish-Purple Leaves)

planting.note: Plant container trees in early spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Trompenburg is more vigorous and heat-tolerant than many red-leaf cultivars, but still benefits from afternoon shade in zone 9 to keep its distinctive leaf color from fading.

directions: Trompenburg, named for the Trompenburg Arboretum in Rotterdam where it was selected, is a vigorous, large-growing upright cultivar distinguished by leaves whose edges roll downward and inward as they mature, giving each leaf a cupped, almost tubular appearance quite different from the flat, deeply cut foliage of most Japanese maples. Leaf color opens deep reddish-purple in spring, holds a bronzed red-purple through summer with better resistance to fading in heat than many red cultivars, and finishes in strong red-orange fall tones. Its size and vigor make it better suited as a specimen shade tree than the compact cultivars typically chosen for small gardens, ultimately reaching well above eye level with an upright, broadly spreading crown. In zone 9, Trompenburg's above-average heat and sun tolerance for a red-leaf cultivar is a real asset, though afternoon shade and deep, infrequent watering during summer still produce the best color and leaf condition.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)

common_name: Bihou Japanese Maple (Golden-Yellow Winter Bark Coral Maple)

planting.note: Plant container trees in early spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; site Bihou where winter sun can reach the trunk and young branches to intensify bark color, and prune out older gray wood periodically since bark color is brightest on young stems.

directions: Bihou is a coral bark-type Japanese maple selected as a companion and alternative to the more common Sango-kaku, distinguished by young bark that colors a bright golden-yellow to greenish-gold rather than Sango-kaku's coral pink-red, an effect that intensifies through winter and provides strong cold-season interest against evergreen backdrops or snow. Leaves are light green through the growing season, smaller and slightly more finely lobed than the species, turning soft gold in fall as the display shifts back to the bark. The habit is upright and vase-shaped, similar in scale to other coral bark cultivars, and like Sango-kaku it colors best on young wood, so periodic renewal pruning of older, grayed stems keeps the winter bark display vivid. In zone 8, afternoon shade and even soil moisture support good leaf quality through summer heat, setting up strong bark color once the leaves drop.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)

common_name: Okushimo Japanese Maple (Upright Columnar Maple with Twisted Curled Foliage)

planting.note: Plant container trees in early spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Okushimo's narrow, upright columnar habit makes it useful for tight spaces where a full-spreading maple would not fit.

directions: Okushimo is grown for its unusual foliage texture: the narrow leaf lobes are twisted, curled, and slightly ruffled along their length, giving the canopy a distinctive shaggy, textured look quite different from the flat, star-shaped leaves of typical Japanese maples, an effect similar in spirit to Shishigashira but on a more open, upright, distinctly columnar tree. New shoots show a coral to pinkish tint that fades as stems mature, adding a secondary point of interest in spring. Green through summer, the foliage turns gold to soft orange in fall. Its narrow, upright growth habit makes Okushimo a useful choice for tight side yards, narrow beds, and vertical accents where a wide-spreading maple would not fit. In zone 8, afternoon shade and consistent moisture keep the curled foliage from scorching at the edges during summer heat.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)

common_name: Coonara Pygmy Japanese Maple (Dwarf Mounding Dissectum Maple)

planting.note: Plant container plants in early spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Coonara Pygmy's small dwarf-mound scale suits raised beds, rock gardens, and containers, and it is slow enough that container culture is a viable long-term option.

directions: Coonara Pygmy is a dwarf, finely dissected-leaf Japanese maple that forms a dense, low, gently mounding shrub rather than the taller weeping fountains typical of most dissectum cultivars, making it one of the more compact lace-leaf maples available. The deeply cut, lacy green leaves are held densely on a slow-growing, twiggy framework, turning shades of orange and gold in fall. Its small mature scale and slow growth rate suit it well to rock gardens, container culture, and the front of mixed borders where the finer texture of dissectum foliage is wanted without the eventual footprint of a full-size weeping maple. In zone 9, afternoon shade and consistent soil moisture protect the fine-textured foliage, which scorches more readily than broader-leaved cultivars under hot, dry, or windy conditions.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)

common_name: Purple Ghost Japanese Maple (Dark-Veined Purple Foliage Maple)

planting.note: Plant container trees in early spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Purple Ghost's dark venation pattern shows best with some direct light rather than deep shade, but protect it from harsh midday and afternoon sun in hot climates.

directions: Purple Ghost is grown for its distinctive foliage pattern: deep purple leaves are overlaid with a network of darker, almost blackish-purple veins that stand out sharply against the lighter purple leaf blade, an effect that has been compared to a 'ghosted' or veined marbling not seen in solid-colored red or purple cultivars like Bloodgood. The upright, moderately spreading habit forms a small to medium tree well suited to use as a specimen or accent where its unusual coloring can be appreciated at close range. Color intensity and vein contrast are both best with some direct morning light; deep shade mutes the pattern while harsh afternoon sun in hot climates can scorch the thinner purple foliage. In zone 8, consistent moisture and afternoon shade during summer heat keep the leaves from fading toward a duller bronze-green.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)
